response_text: The initial process involves the user defining a thread function such as a print function that takes a void* argument. After that, a struct is created containing the necessary data, initializes it, then passes a pointer to it into the osCreateThread function. Then the osCreateThread function creates a thread stack involving the different registers like PC, LR, R0-3, simulating the CPU state. Since, PC holds the address of the thread function, the thread function is placed in Register R0’s position. Placing the argument in R0 works because of the calling convention defined by the system's Application Binary Interface (ABI) on ARM-based systems. This convention is specifically the ARM Procedure Call Standard (AAPCS) on ARM-based systems. The convention applies as when a function is called, its first argument must be placed in register R0. When the thread is scheduled to run, the OS sets the Process Stack Pointer (PSP) to point to the thread stack and triggers a context switch where the CPU loads the values from the stack into the appropriate registers through decrementing a stack pointer. Therefore, R0 will be assigned the correct function of which the CPU can execute. This process and behaviour lead to arguments being able to be passed into threads effectively.\n
